newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU slaps restrictions on Burma contacts.
newsitem.headline: EU slaps restrictions on Burma contacts.

text.p: The European Union on Monday imposed strict limits on contacts with Burmese officials and their families in response to what the 15-nation bloc sees as Burma's continuing failure to respect human rights.
EU foreign ministers agreed the move -- part of a gradual build-up of pressure on Rangoon's military government -- without debate.
"There is a very serious situation in Burma with a lack of respect for human rights and democracy," Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring told Reuters. "Today's decision reflects our concern."

Spring, whose country is current EU president, discussed the EU's position with Burmese Foreign Minister Ohn Gyaw in September on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly, but diplomats said the talks went nowhere.

The new sanctions bar visas to members of Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) and their families, and to senior members of the military and security forces viewed by the EU as impeding the transition to democracy.
High-level EU visits to Burma by ministers and senior officials are also to be suspended.
In a statement, the ministers said the SLORC had failed "to demonstrate any willingness to respond to the concerns of the United Nations General Assembly and the European Union".
"Further measures may need to be considered," they added.
The EU has already imposed a number of restrictions on Burma, including an arms embargo and the suspension of non-humanitarian aid and development programmes.
Diplomats said further measures could include economic restrictions, but they emphasised that moves in that direction were a long way off.
"There would have to be a severe deterioration (in Burma) and moves by the United States," said one diplomat.

Some EU countries have been reluctant to take stringent actions against Rangoon without similar actions from Washington and the United Nations. The United States recently barred entry visas to SLORC officials.
Burma's military government has sparked international anger over its crackdown on democracy activists.
This came to a head last week when it detained Kyi Maung, a 75-year-old official in the National League for Democracy (NLD), the party of Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.
Suu Kyi has called for the EU and others to impose a strict trade embargo on Burma.
NLD sources said on Monday that Kyi Maung had now been released. He had been held for a suspected role in a student sit-in protest.

The EU has been slowly turning up the heat on the SLORC since earlier this year when Denmark began lobbying for action following the death in a Burmese prison of James Leander Nichols, its unaccredited honorary consul.
Nichols, who also represented EU member Finland and non-members Norway and Switzerland, was Suu Kyi's godfather.
